Sylvester Prierias
sĭl-vĕs´tẽr prĭ-ĕr´ĭ-as
n. (Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio, c. 1456–1527, Dominican Master of the Sacred Palace, who wrote the first official Roman reply to the Ninety-Five Theses)
Latin Prierias, of Prierio in Piedmont; Sylvester, of the woods.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sylvester Prierias held the office of Master of the Sacred Palace, the papal theologian, and in 1518 produced the Dialogus against Luther — Rome's first formal answer, written, he boasted, in three days. Its argument is not exegetical but jurisdictional, and it is valuable for its candour. The universal church, he wrote, is virtually the Roman church; the Roman church is virtually the pope; therefore whoever does not rest on the teaching of the Roman church and the Roman pontiff as the infallible rule of faith is a heretic. He did not attempt to show from Scripture that indulgences are lawful; he asserted that the question was settled by who had spoken. Luther said the Dialogus taught him more than its author intended. Mar 7:9 is the Lord's own judgment on that order of authority — “Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition” — and Mat 15:9 its result, “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” Isa 29:13 describes a fear of God “taught by the precept of men.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines tradition as the delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; and infallible as not capable of error.

expand to see more

TRADI'TION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; the transmission of any opinions or practice from forefathers to descendants by oral communication.

2. That which is handed down from age to age by oral communication.

INFAL'LIBLE, a. Not fallible; not capable of erring; entirely exempt from liability to mistake.

Key Scripture

Mar 7:9 — "And he said unto them, Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition."

Mat 15:9 — "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men."

Isa 29:13 — "Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:"

Col 2:22 — "Which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men?"

Modern Corruption

Prierias stated the papal claim more plainly than any apologist since, and the plainness is the refutation.

expand to see more

The Dialogus is the formal principle of Rome without embarrassment: the church is the pope, and the pope is the rule of faith. Later Roman writing has softened the formula and surrounded it with qualifications, but Prierias had no reason to be careful in 1518, and what he wrote is the premise on which the indulgence traffic, the treasury of merits and the whole apparatus rested. Once stated, it can be tested, and Mar 7:9 tests it: a tradition that overrides the commandment of God is not a development of it. Col 2:22 dismisses “the commandments and doctrines of men” as things “to perish with the using.”

The formal principle of the Reformation is the direct contrary, and it is not a Protestant invention but the Lord's own practice: He answered the Sadducees from Moses, the lawyers from the law, and the devil from Deuteronomy. Isa 29:13 warns what happens to worship when the fear of God is “taught by the precept of men” — it becomes lip-service with the heart removed. The recovery is Scripture as the only infallible rule, with tradition honoured as a witness and never seated as a judge.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek paradosis (G3862), a tradition, that which is handed over; entalma (G1778), a commandment of men; mataios (G3152), vain.

Greek paradosis (G3862) — tradition, that which is delivered; Mark 7:9.

Greek atheteo (G114) — to set aside, to reject; Mark 7:9.

Greek entalma (G1778) — an injunction, a commandment of men; Matthew 15:9.

Greek mataios (G3152) — vain, empty; Matthew 15:9.

Hebrew mitsvah (H4687) — a commandment, a precept; Isaiah 29:13.

Usage

"“Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition” (Mar 7:9) — the order he defended."

"“teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) — the Dialogus in a clause."

"“their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men” (Isa 29:13) — the worship it produces."
